title: NanoSurge
oneLiner: A 3D multi agent simulation where autonomous nanobots learn to hunt infections inside the human bloodstream using reinforcement learning.

sections.title: Why NanoSurge exists
sections.text: NanoSurge began as my MSc dissertation, but I deliberately wanted it to be more than a typical final project. After working on several traditional game systems, I wanted to explore something unfamiliar and risky. Around that time, I was playing AAA games that used learning based AI rather than predictable behaviour, which pushed me towards reinforcement learning. Discovering multi agent reinforcement learning changed everything. An idea that agents could learn movement, navigation and combat without gameplay scripts felt too powerful to ignore.

sections.title: From ideas to a risky direction
sections.text: Early concepts ranged from rescue drones navigating disaster zones to robots solving mazes. None of them felt exciting enough to justify the learning curve of MARL. The breakthrough came after encountering research discussions about nanobots being used for medical treatment. While the real world application is speculative, the idea of autonomous agents navigating blood vessels to eliminate infections felt immediately compelling as a simulation and a game system.

sections.title: Building a learning environment, not scripted AI
sections.text: Unlike traditional enemy AI, NanoSurge avoids hardcoded behaviour. Nanobots and virus agents are placed inside a flowing bloodstream environment and learn through interaction alone. Movement, pursuit, and combat are not explicitly programmed. Instead, agents learn through reward signals, collisions, and spatial constraints, making their behaviour unpredictable but emergent.

sections.title: When everything broke
sections.text: The most difficult phase was agent training. Early runs failed entirely agents exploited reward loopholes, drifted endlessly, or ignored objectives. Poor reward balance caused agents to optimise the wrong behaviours, while small YAML configuration mistakes invalidated days of training. With less than a month remaining before submission, the core idea that earned project approval was still unstable.

sections.title: Features that didn’t survive
sections.text: Two major systems were cut due to instability and time constraints. Virus agents were designed to multiply into groups, increasing difficulty dynamically, while nanobots could call nearby agents for assistance. Both systems worked in isolation but introduced learning instability at scale, causing agents to break environmental constraints or abandon objectives. Rather than force unfinished mechanics, these systems were intentionally removed to preserve training integrity.

sections.title: What would I rebuild next
sections.text: With more time, I would reintroduce virus multiplication and nanobot regrouping incrementally, focusing on stability before complexity. Understanding why agents escaped the vessel or stalled during regrouping is now a clear next step. These systems remain the most exciting extension points for future versions of NanoSurge.

sections.title: Why this project mattered to me
sections.text: NanoSurge was my first deep dive into machine learning for games, and it fundamentally changed how I think about AI. Watching agents learn behaviours I never explicitly coded was both frustrating and fascinating. More importantly, it gave me confidence that I can design learning based systems, not just scripted gameplay. This project opened the door to future work where AI behaviour emerges rather than being predefined.

title: Wreckfest
oneLiner: A small online multiplayer vehicle combat prototype focused on control feel, role based gameplay, and network safe systems.

sections.title: Why Wreckfest exists
sections.text: Wreckfest was developed as part of a Connected Games Development module, but my personal goal went beyond completing coursework. I had never built an online multiplayer game before and wanted to understand how real time gameplay systems behave once networking, authority, and synchronisation are involved. The project became a focused attempt to close that skill gap rather than build a content heavy game.

sections.title: Finding the right idea
sections.text: Early brainstorming involved familiar ideas like tactical shooters and survival games, but these felt overused and risky within the timeline. Inspiration came from cooperative vehicle based games, combining the movement intensity of arcade driving with turret based combat. The final concept revolved around two teams, each vehicle controlled by two players: one driving and one shooting with the ability to swap roles mid match.

sections.title: Designing for feel before features
sections.text: Most development time was spent tuning vehicle movement and handling. Two distinct vehicles were implemented a heavier muscle car and a lighter minivan each with different acceleration, turning, and drifting behaviour. A ScriptableObject driven setup allowed the same controller logic to support multiple vehicles while keeping balance manageable. Player testing and feedback cycles were critical to achieving readable and satisfying handling.

sections.title: Camera, weapons, and combat
sections.text: Camera behaviour was deliberately split by role. Drivers received a wider view of the vehicle and environment, while shooters were given a tighter, turret focused perspective to prioritise aiming. Turret combat initially used projectile physics but was replaced with raycast based shooting to reduce network lag and improve consistency. A high damage rocket launcher was added as a high risk weapon with a long cooldown, encouraging timing and coordination.

sections.title: When multiplayer broke everything
sections.text: Converting single player mechanics to multiplayer revealed major flaws. Without proper ownership handling, players could control multiple cars, drive and shoot simultaneously, or end up on opposing teams while sharing a vehicle. These issues required restarting large parts of the implementation and forced a deeper understanding of authority, ServerRPCs, and ClientRPCs. This phase reshaped how I approach system design in networked games.

sections.title: Environmental complexity and optimisation
sections.text: To increase gameplay depth, a sandstorm mechanic was introduced that dynamically altered vehicle behaviour during matches. This added unpredictability and environmental pressure, which was highlighted positively during evaluation. Performance optimisation was equally important, the arena map was heavily reworked by removing unseen geometry, unnecessary colliders, excess shadows, and introducing LODs, resulting in a significant FPS improvement.

sections.title: What I kept small, on purpose
sections.text: Only two vehicles and one map were included in the final build. This was a deliberate decision to maintain balance, reduce asset instability, and ensure mechanics were fully playable rather than partially implemented. Future content was scoped clearly but not forced into an already tight timeline.

sections.title: What comes next?
sections.text: If extended further, Wreckfest would focus on expanding weapon variety, introducing new arenas with unique environmental effects, and improving damage feedback and power ups. With stronger networking foundations in place, future iterations would prioritise depth without sacrificing clarity or performance.

title: Endless Cruiser VR
oneLiner: An endless car driving prototype that experiments with adaptive traffic using Q-learning and later evolved into a VR driving experience.

sections.title: Why Endless Cruiser exists
sections.text: Endless Cruiser was developed during my early game development journey as part of a 3D Games Programming module. I deliberately chose an endless driving format to keep the core gameplay simple while experimenting with advanced concepts like reinforcement learning and virtual reality. The goal was not to build a large game, but to create a controlled environment where I could learn, fail, and iterate.

sections.title: Adaptive traffic instead of random spawning
sections.text: Rather than relying on purely random obstacle spawning, I experimented with Q-learning to influence how NPC cars appeared on the road. The idea was to create adaptive traffic that responded to the player’s lane position, rewarding situations that increased challenge and penalising congestion that felt unfair. While imperfect, this approach introduced unpredictability beyond traditional scripted logic.

sections.title: What actually happened with Q-learning
sections.text: In practice, the Q-table increased difficulty but also revealed its limitations. NPC cars frequently spawned in the player’s lane, sometimes creating one sided traffic patterns. Despite this, the system demonstrated learning behaviour by consistently placing obstacles ahead of the player to maximise challenge. Seeing an AI driven system influence gameplay in my second ever game was a major milestone in my learning process.

sections.title: Transitioning from 3D to VR
sections.text: The project initially began as a standard 3D game. Once the core systems were functional, VR support was introduced to explore immersion and driving realism. The shift fundamentally changed the experience: high speed driving became more intense, and even simple mechanics felt significantly more impactful when viewed from inside the vehicle.

sections.title: VR challenges and performance fixes
sections.text: VR introduced major challenges, including inconsistent camera positioning, performance drops, and early motion sickness. Continuous object instantiation caused low frame rates, so an object pooling system was implemented to recycle NPC cars efficiently. Vehicles behind the player were returned to the pool and reused ahead of the player, significantly improving FPS and reducing discomfort.

sections.title: What I’m proud of
sections.text: As one of my earliest projects, Endless Cruiser represents my first successful integration of reinforcement learning, VR, and performance optimisation in a single prototype. Implementing a Q-table and a VR driving experience this early in my journey gave me confidence to take on more complex systems in later projects.

sections.title: Lessons that shaped later projects
sections.text: This project highlighted the importance of clean code structure, separation of responsibilities, and choosing the right tools early. Poor abstraction and overloading scripts became clear pain points. These lessons directly influenced how I structured and approached subsequent projects, leading to more maintainable and scalable systems.

title: Threshold
oneLiner: Break out of the basement, unlock the mansion, and outsmart the keeper before you’re dragged back into the dark.

sections.title: Why Threshold exists
sections.text: I love tense, atmospheric first-person experiences, and I wanted to build an escape game where tension comes from peeling back layers of confinement rather than simple jump scares. Threshold started as a pure passion project to explore classic escape-room puzzles set in a sprawling, locked-down mansion. The core goal was to take the player from a small victory—escaping a basement cell—straight into the realization that the entire isolated estate is an even larger cage.

sections.title: The core gameplay loop
sections.text: The game focuses on first-person exploration, observation, and logical problem solving. The player starts with zero context in a subterranean cell and must inspect their surroundings to find an initial way out. Once in the main mansion, progress relies on discovering clues, managing inventory items, and cracking distinct lock types to gradually open new wings of the house while uncovering why this place exists.

sections.title: Interactive puzzle mechanics
sections.text: To keep the escape room feel tactile, I built a modular interaction system covering multiple lock and puzzle types. Current mechanics include physical key-and-lock doors, numeric keypads with custom code validation, and multi-dial combination locks. Each system is designed to plug directly into an inventory manager, letting the player inspect collected items and apply solutions seamlessly.

sections.title: Designing tension & the patrolling AI
sections.text: Puzzles alone can feel static, so the next major milestone is an active pursuer AI. The moment the player breaches the basement, a patrolling entity begins sweeping the estate. Rather than an instant game-over, the AI is designed to capture the player and drag them back to the basement cell, resetting physical room states while keeping the player's mental knowledge intact. This turns every lock-picking attempt into a high-stakes race against time.

sections.title: Current status & road ahead
sections.text: Threshold is currently a functional prototype with core first-person movement, an inventory system, and working locks in-engine. As of now, players can search for hidden keys to unlock doors and crack safe combinations, with several more complex, multi-step mechanical puzzles actively under development. Because this is an ongoing passion project driven by my love for building games, the next major milestones include rolling out these new puzzle types, implementing the NavMesh-driven pursuer AI, and expanding the environmental storytelling.

title: Missing Reference Finder
oneLiner: An internal Unity Editor Diagnostic Tool designed to automate project-wide audits, identifying corrupted object references and unlinked scripts across scenes and prefabs before build deployment.

sections.title: Why I'm building this tool
sections.text: As Unity projects grow, renaming files, moving folders, and deleting old assets frequently breaks component references under the hood. I started building this tool as a pre-flight check before testing or compiling builds, with the goal of catching missing links and broken scripts before they turn into runtime null reference errors.

sections.title: The core problem to solve
sections.text: Checking every scene and prefab by hand is slow and unreliable, especially since some broken references appear empty while secretly holding missing asset IDs. I wanted to build a simple Editor Window that automates this check across the Assets folder instead of relying on manual inspection.

sections.title: Implementing safe scene and prefab scanning
sections.text: To scan scenes without disrupting active work in the editor, I set up the tool to load scenes additively in the background, inspect the root objects, and close them when finished. For prefabs, the tool traverses the hierarchy recursively to ensure child objects aren't skipped.

sections.title: Working with Unity's Serialization
sections.text: Rather than standard reflection, I used SerializedObject and SerializedProperty to read Unity's raw serialized data directly. The tool identifies missing references by checking for null object references that still contain a non-zero instance ID, alongside null-checks for missing MonoScripts.

sections.title: Current scope & early limitations
sections.text: The prototype currently focuses solely on .prefab and .unity files within the project's Assets directory. It outputs findings to a scrollable IMGUI list inside a custom EditorWindow so broken assets can be reviewed in one place.

sections.title: What I'm working on next
sections.text: Because the tool is still under active development, the next steps are adding clickable entries that ping broken objects directly in the hierarchy, expanding checks to ScriptableObjects and Materials, and refining the scanning performance on larger asset sets.
